summary: Provides an information model for Abstraction and Control of TE Networks, describing the kinds of objects and relationships used by the ACTN framework.

eli5.summary: This is the list of parts and how they connect, like a blueprint for the building blocks of the ACTN framework.

questions: how does actn coordinate multi-domain networks
what is a virtual network in actn
subtitle: The structure and objects for abstracting and controlling multi-domain traffic engineering networks.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a way to control and abstract traffic engineering across multiple domains and service levels, from customers requesting services to the underlying physical network.
tldr.mechanism: ACTN defines an information model describing primitives (operations), objects (data structures), and their relationships across three tiers: Customer Network Controllers (CNCs), a Multi-Domain Service Coordinator (MDSC), and Provisioning Network Controllers (PNCs).
tldr.outcome: Operators can request and manage virtual networks at a high level while the MDSC translates and coordinates those requests with underlying domains, enabling multi-domain service delivery.

today: RFC 8454 is an Informational RFC that provides the information model for the ACTN framework specified in RFC 8453. It is implemented in YANG data models for actual control plane deployments in multi-domain networks.

sections.title: Three-Tier Architecture
sections.content:
ACTN defines a three-tier control hierarchy that separates network service requests from network implementation. At the top are Customer Network Controllers (CNCs) representing customer applications and services. At the bottom are Provisioning Network Controllers (PNCs) managing individual network domains. Between them sits the Multi-Domain Service Coordinator (MDSC), which translates customer service requests into domain-specific traffic engineering operations.

The MDSC connects to CNCs via the CMI (CNC-MDSC Interface), where customers request virtual networks in service terms. The MDSC connects to PNCs via the MPI (MDSC-PNC Interface), where it coordinates traffic engineering at the domain level. The RFC models both interfaces as a common interface type, since MDSC-to-MDSC communication in hierarchical deployments follows the same pattern.

This separation allows customers to express requirements without knowing network internals, and allows the MDSC to apply policies and abstraction to present each customer with a customized view of available resources.
sections.eli5: The system has three levels: customers at the top asking for services, network domains at the bottom doing the real work, and a coordinator in the middle translating requests from customer language to domain language and back.

sections.title: Virtual Network and Traffic Engineering Primitives
sections.content:
The information model defines two types of primitives depending on which interface they operate at. Virtual Network (VN) primitives operate at the CMI between CNCs and MDSCs. They include VN Instantiate (create a new service), VN Modify (change an existing service), VN Delete (tear down a service), VN Update (push topology changes to customers), VN Compute (forecast feasibility without committing), and VN Query (pull the current topology view).

Traffic Engineering (TE) primitives operate at the MPI between MDSCs and PNCs. They include TE Instantiate/Modify/Delete for managing tunnels in network domains, TE Topology Update (pushing domain topology and resource information to the MDSC), and Path Compute (requesting path computation from a domain).

This separation reflects the different levels of abstraction: customers think in terms of virtual network services and connectivity types (point-to-point, point-to-multipoint, multipoint-to-multipoint), while domain controllers think in terms of specific tunnels, resource constraints, and routing metrics.
sections.eli5: The model defines two sets of instructions: ones customers use to ask for services, and ones domains use to actually build those services. The coordinator translates between them.

sections.title: Virtual Network Objects and Service Characteristics
sections.content:
VN objects describe the service request from a customer perspective. Every VN has a unique identifier and service characteristics that specify what the customer needs. VN Service Characteristics include the connectivity type (P2P, P2MP, MP2MP, MP2P, or multi-destination), directionality (unidirectional or bidirectional), and a traffic matrix defining bandwidth and constraints.

VN constraints can include layer protocol (MPLS, ODU, OCh), diversity requirements (keep this VN separate from another), metrics (cost, delay, latency), and objective functions. VN Survivability describes recovery requirements: unprotected, per-tunnel protection (0:1, 1+1, 1:1, 1:N, M:N), or on-the-fly restoration. VN Survivability Policy allows customers to delegate decisions to the MDSC, such as whether local reroutes are permitted or whether the MDSC can proactively update the customer when topology changes.

Endpoints identify which nodes in the network the VN connects. VN topology describes how virtual nodes and virtual links relate to each other, providing customers with an abstracted view of the underlying service.
sections.eli5: When a customer asks for a service, they describe what they need: where to connect, how much data, how reliable it should be, and how quickly it should respond. The coordinator understands these requirements and figures out how to build them in the real network.

sections.title: Traffic Engineering Objects and Domain Resources
sections.content:
TE objects describe network-level tunnels and resources. The RFC defines TE Tunnel Characteristics that specify tunnels in domain terms: specific source and destination nodes, routing constraints, metrics, and protection types. TE topology includes detailed information about network nodes, links, and termination points, along with interface capabilities (what switching layers each port supports).

TE Topology Update allows domain controllers to advertise either their complete topology or an abstracted view determined by policy and agreements with the MDSC. The RFC references [TE-TOPO] (YANG data models for TE topology) for detailed specifications of node attributes, link attributes, and termination point capabilities. This abstraction is crucial: the MDSC might receive only an abstracted view of a domain's internal topology, hiding details while preserving the information needed for path computation and service placement.

Path Compute Request/Reply allows the MDSC to ask a domain controller to compute a path given source, destination, and constraints. The domain responds with one or more candidate paths.
sections.eli5: The network domains describe their internal structure: which routers and links they have, what they can do, and how much capacity they have. This lets the coordinator figure out where to put the customer's service.

sections.title: Mapping Between Service and Domain Layers
sections.content:
The information model maps VN primitives to VN objects and TE primitives to TE objects. For example, a VN Instantiate request carries VN Service Characteristics and endpoint information. The MDSC translates this into one or more TE Instantiate requests to domain controllers, each carrying TE Tunnel Characteristics specific to that domain.

A VN Modify request to change bandwidth or add diversity constraints becomes a TE Modify request to each affected domain. VN Topology Update (MDSC pushing changes to customers) reflects changes in the underlying TE topology. VN Compute returns a candidate VN topology by asking domains to compute paths and assembling them into an end-to-end service view.

Critically, the model separates what customers express from what happens behind the scenes. The same VN service request could result in different TE implementations depending on domain policies, network state, and objectives. This abstraction is essential for multi-domain scaling: customers do not need to understand every domain's internals, and domains can evolve independently.
sections.eli5: The coordinator translates: when a customer asks for a service, the coordinator breaks it into instructions for each domain. When a domain reports a change, the coordinator tells the customer what it means for their service.
